title: Composition of Congress
ask: How is Congress composed under Art. VI, Secs. 1, 2 and 5(1)–(2)?
items: Bicameral: a Senate and a House of Representatives
Legislative power vested in Congress except to the extent reserved to the people by initiative and referendum
Senate: twenty-four Senators elected at large by the qualified voters, as may be provided by law
House: not more than 250 members, ‘unless otherwise fixed by law’
District representatives: elected from legislative districts apportioned among provinces, cities and Metro Manila
Party-list representatives: elected through a party-list system of registered national, regional and sectoral parties or organizations
Party-list representatives constitute twenty per centum (20%) of the total number of representatives, including those under the party list

title: Qualifications of a Senator
ask: What are the five qualifications of a Senator (Art. VI, Sec. 3)?
items: Natural-born citizen of the Philippines
At least thirty-five years of age on the day of the election
Able to read and write
A registered voter
Resident of the Philippines for not less than two years immediately preceding the day of the election
src: Art. VI, Sec. 3
hook: Age and residence are reckoned on/before election day, not at proclamation or assumption.

title: Qualifications of a district Representative
ask: What are the five qualifications of a Member of the House (Art. VI, Sec. 6)?
items: Natural-born citizen of the Philippines
At least twenty-five years of age on the day of the election
Able to read and write
Except party-list representatives: a registered voter in the district in which he shall be elected
Except party-list representatives: a resident of that district for not less than one year immediately preceding the day of the election
src: Art. VI, Sec. 6

title: Qualifications of a party-list nominee
ask: What are the qualifications of a party-list nominee under RA 7941, Sec. 9?
items: Natural-born citizen of the Philippines
Registered voter
Resident of the Philippines for not less than one year immediately preceding the day of the election
Able to read and write
Bona fide member of the party or organization for at least ninety days preceding the day of the election
At least twenty-five years of age on the day of the election
Youth-sector nominee: at least 25 but not more than 30 on election day; may finish the term if he turns 30
src: RA 7941, Sec. 9; Art. VI, Sec. 6 (party-list nominees exempt from the district voter and residence rules)

title: Terms and term limits of Members of Congress
ask: What are the rules on the terms and term limits of Senators and Representatives (Art. VI, Secs. 4, 7)?
items: Senators: term of six years
Representatives (district and party-list): term of three years
Both terms begin, unless otherwise provided by law, at noon on the thirtieth day of June next following the election
No Senator shall serve for more than two consecutive terms
No Representative shall serve for more than three consecutive terms
Voluntary renunciation of the office for any length of time is not an interruption in the continuity of service for the full term
One elected in a special election serves only the unexpired term (Sec. 9)
src: Art. VI, Secs. 4, 7, 9

title: Congress cannot add qualifications
ask: What are the rules on whether Congress may add qualifications for members of Congress?
items: The qualifications in Secs. 3 and 6 are exclusive; Congress cannot add to them, directly or indirectly
SJS v. DDB (2008): mandatory drug testing of senatorial candidates was void because it added a qualification
A law disqualifying candidates for doing or omitting something not in the Constitution (e.g., skipping debates) is void
Exception: ‘as provided by law’ in Sec. 5(1) lets Congress set party-list nominee qualifications (Albano)
That power covers only party-list representatives, not district representatives or Senators (Albano)
Party-list restrictions must still pass equal protection and due process (Albano)
Local offices: qualifications are statutory, so Congress has more room, but conditions must be reasonable
src: Art. VI, Secs. 3, 5(1), 6; SJS v. DDB (2008, Gatmaytan’s book); Albano v. COMELEC (2023)

title: Apportionment of legislative districts
ask: What are the constitutional rules on apportioning legislative districts (Art. VI, Sec. 5(1), (3), (4)) and who may create them?
items: Apportioned among the provinces, cities and the Metropolitan Manila area
In accordance with the number of their respective inhabitants
On the basis of a uniform and progressive ratio
Each district: as far as practicable, contiguous, compact and adjacent territory
Each city with a population of at least 250,000 has at least one representative
Each province, regardless of population, has at least one representative
Congress must reapportion within three years following the return of every census
Only Congress, by law, creates districts; so a regional assembly cannot create provinces or cities (Sema)
The 250 cap may be exceeded by law, including piecemeal laws creating districts (Mariano; BANAT)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 5(1), (3), (4); Sema v. COMELEC; Mariano v. COMELEC (Gatmaytan’s book)
hook: The standards exist to prevent gerrymandering (Bernas).

title: Sectoral seats under the transitory clause
ask: For three consecutive terms after ratification, half of the party-list seats were filled from which sectors (Art. VI, Sec. 5(2))?
items: Labor
Peasant
Urban poor
Indigenous cultural communities
Women
Youth
Such other sectors as may be provided by law
Except the religious sector
src: Art. VI, Sec. 5(2)
hook: Filled ‘by selection or election’, as provided by law; the religious sector is the one express exclusion.

title: Sectors listed in RA 7941
ask: Which sectors does RA 7941, Sec. 5 enumerate for sectoral parties, and is the list exclusive?
items: Labor and peasant
Fisherfolk and urban poor
Indigenous cultural communities and elderly
Handicapped and women
Youth and veterans
Overseas workers and professionals
The enumeration is not exclusive (Ang Ladlad)
src: RA 7941, Sec. 5; Ang Ladlad v. COMELEC

title: Atong Paglaum parameters
ask: What are the six parameters for party-list participation laid down in Atong Paglaum?
items: Three groups may participate: national, regional and sectoral parties or organizations
National and regional parties need not organize along sectoral lines or represent the ‘marginalized and underrepresented’
Political parties may join by registering under the party-list system and fielding no district candidates
A party with district candidates joins only through a separately registered sectoral wing linked by coalition
Sectoral parties may be ‘marginalized and underrepresented’ or lack ‘well-defined political constituencies’; principal advocacy for the sector suffices
Majority of a sectoral party’s members must belong to the sector
Sectoral nominees must belong to the sector or have a track record of advocacy for it
Nominees of national and regional parties must be bona fide members
A party is not disqualified for some disqualified nominees if at least one nominee remains qualified
src: Atong Paglaum v. COMELEC (2013) (items 3–4 are parameter 3; items 6–8 are parameter 5)
hook: Sereno, C.J., dissenting: the system is a social-justice tool; national parties now ‘invade’ the space of the marginalized.

title: Why Atong Paglaum opened the party-list
ask: What grounds did Atong Paglaum give for reading the party-list system as not exclusively sectoral?
items: Party-list representation is not synonymous with sectoral representation
The framers rejected reserved sectoral seats (the 19–22 vote)
The text’s commas — ‘national, regional, and sectoral parties’ — name three distinct groups
Sectoral parties were meant to be a part, not the entirety, of the system
Ang Bagong Bayani and BANAT guidelines limiting it to the marginalized were abandoned
src: Atong Paglaum v. COMELEC; Gatmaytan’s book; DG reviewer

title: Grounds to refuse or cancel party-list registration
ask: What are the eight grounds under RA 7941, Sec. 6 for COMELEC to refuse or cancel a party-list group’s registration (after due notice and hearing)?
items: It is a religious sect or denomination, or organized for religious purposes
It advocates violence or unlawful means to seek its goal
It is a foreign party or organization
It receives support from a foreign government, party, foundation or organization for partisan election purposes
It violates or fails to comply with laws, rules or regulations relating to elections
It declares untruthful statements in its petition
It has ceased to exist for at least one year
It failed to participate in the last two elections, or to get 2% of party-list votes in the two preceding elections
src: RA 7941, Sec. 6; An Waray (ground 5); Abang Lingkod (ground 6)

title: Limits on COMELEC in party-list registration
ask: What limits do the cases place on COMELEC when it denies or cancels party-list registration?
items: No track record required of the group; principal advocacy for the sector suffices (Abang Lingkod)
Track record matters only for nominees who do not belong to the sector (Abang Lingkod)
Misrepresentation justifies cancellation only if it relates to a qualification (Abang Lingkod)
No denial on moral or religious grounds; citing the Bible and Koran violates non-establishment (Ang Ladlad)
Moral disapproval of an unpopular minority is not a legitimate state interest (Ang Ladlad)
Notice and hearing are indispensable before cancellation (Senior Citizens)
An unimplemented term-sharing covenant is not a ground for cancellation (Senior Citizens)
src: Abang Lingkod v. COMELEC; Ang Ladlad v. COMELEC; Senior Citizens v. COMELEC

title: Rules on the list of party-list nominees
ask: What are the rules on the list of nominees under RA 7941, Sec. 8, and why must there be at least five?
items: List of not less than five names
Submitted not later than 45 days before the election
A person may be nominated in one list only, and only with written consent
No candidate for any elective office may be on the list
The ban on persons who lost in the immediately preceding election was struck down (Albano)
No change of names or order after submission, except when a nominee dies, withdraws in writing, or becomes incapacitated
The substitute nominee is placed last on the list
Purpose of five names: inform voters who stands behind the group; provide for vacancies (COCOFED)
Failing to submit five is a ground to cancel; the ‘one qualified nominee’ rule does not excuse it (COCOFED)
src: RA 7941, Sec. 8; COCOFED v. COMELEC; Albano v. COMELEC

title: Duterte Youth rulings on substitution
ask: What did Duterte Youth v. COMELEC hold on withdrawal and substitution of party-list nominees?
items: RA 7941 does not prohibit withdrawal as such; COMELEC merely notes it
What is prohibited is changing names or order of nominees, except death, written withdrawal or incapacity
Substitution deadlines stay mandatory even after the election
Timing is substance: voters have a right to know the nominees before voting
Sec. 16 (vacancy filled from the list) applies only to a vacancy during the term, not a list exhausted before the seat exists
COMELEC keeps jurisdiction until the nominee validly assumes office
The en masse post-election substitution was grave abuse and void
src: Duterte Youth v. COMELEC (2024)

title: Party-list seat, vacancy and affiliation rules
ask: What are the rules on a sitting party-list representative’s seat, affiliation and vacancy (RA 7941, Secs. 15–16 and cases)?
items: Changing political party or sectoral affiliation during the term forfeits the seat
Changing affiliation within six months before an election makes him ineligible as nominee of the new group
A vacancy is filled automatically by the next nominee in the order submitted
The replacement serves only the unexpired term
If the list is exhausted, the group submits additional nominees
Bona fide membership in the group is a continuing qualification (Lico)
Term-sharing among nominees is void ab initio: contrary to the three-year term (Sec. 7) and public policy (Senior Citizens)
src: RA 7941, Secs. 15–16; Art. VI, Sec. 7; Lico; Senior Citizens

title: Albano v. COMELEC points
ask: What are the key points of Albano v. COMELEC (2023) on party-list nominee restrictions?
items: ‘As provided by law’ in Sec. 5(1) lets Congress prescribe party-list nominee qualifications and mechanics
That power does not extend to district representatives or Senators
Restrictions must satisfy equal protection and due process
The ban on nominees who lost in the immediately preceding election was void
Arbitrary: no clear link between losing an election and abusing the party-list system
Arbitrary: it barred only losers of the most recent election, not earlier ones
Arbitrary: losers could still run for district seats but not as party-list nominees
src: Albano v. COMELEC (2023)

title: Who decides party-list disputes: COMELEC or HRET
ask: Which forum decides each kind of party-list dispute?
items: Registration and cancellation of the group, even one with a sitting member: COMELEC (An Waray)
Intra-party leadership disputes and nominations before assumption: COMELEC (Lokin)
Withdrawal and substitution of nominees: COMELEC, applying mandatory deadlines (Duterte Youth)
Qualifications of a candidate before he becomes a Member: COMELEC (Marcos)
Qualifications or expulsion from the party of a sitting member: HRET (Lico)
src: Lokin; Lico; An Waray; Duterte Youth; Marcos v. COMELEC

title: An Waray points
ask: What did An Waray v. COMELEC (2024) hold on cancelling a party-list group with a sitting member?
items: COMELEC, not the HRET, cancels registration even if the group holds a seat
The group, not its nominee, is the respondent, so HRET jurisdiction over Members is not engaged
Registration is a privilege akin to a franchise that never becomes final against the State
So COMELEC’s power to revoke registration does not prescribe
Seating a nominee without COMELEC proclamation seriously violates RA 7941, Sec. 13
Defying the final seat allocation is a violation of election laws under Sec. 6(5)
src: An Waray Party-List v. COMELEC (2024)

title: BANAT seat allocation formula
ask: What are the steps for allocating party-list seats under BANAT, as refined by Araro and AKMA-PTM?
items: Total party-list seats = (number of district seats ÷ 0.80) × 0.20
Rank all groups from highest to lowest votes
Compute each group’s percentage of total valid party-list votes (Araro divisor)
Each group with at least 2% gets one guaranteed seat
Remaining seats × each group’s percentage; the whole number is its additional seats (fractions dropped)
Then one seat each down the ranking until all seats are filled
No 2% threshold in the additional-seat round (BANAT; AKMA-PTM)
No group gets more than three seats
COMELEC may proclaim despite uncanvassed votes that can no longer affect the result (AKMA-PTM; OEC Sec. 233)
src: RA 7941, Sec. 11; BANAT v. COMELEC (2009); Araro; AKMA-PTM

title: Araro divisor: what counts
ask: Under Araro, what is included in and excluded from the divisor for party-list percentages?
items: Included: total valid votes cast for the party-list system
Included: valid votes for groups on the ballot that are disqualified later
Excluded: spoiled and invalid votes
Excluded: votes for groups disqualified with finality and made known to voters before the election
Reason: a later disqualification cannot invalidate votes of voters who relied on the official ballot
The rule applies prospectively
src: Araro v. COMELEC (2013)

title: Requisites for change of domicile
ask: What three requisites must concur for a candidate to change domicile (Aquino; Marcos)?
items: Actual removal to, or bodily presence in, the new place
A bona fide intention to abandon the old domicile (and remain in the new one)
Definite acts consistent with that intention
src: Aquino v. COMELEC (1995); Marcos v. COMELEC (1995); see also Gallego; Romualdez v. RTC
hook: Without clear and positive proof of all three, the domicile of origin continues.

title: Domicile rules for congressional candidates
ask: What are the rules on residence (domicile) of candidates drawn from Aquino, Marcos and Mangudadatu?
items: Residence in election law means domicile
Leasing a condominium unit shows intent to lease, not a permanent home (Aquino)
The one-year residence rule applies even to a newly created district (Aquino)
A minor follows the parents’ domicile (Marcos)
Absence to work, study or for other temporary purposes does not lose domicile (Marcos)
A wife does not lose her domicile of origin by marriage (Marcos)
A mistake in the COC does not defeat actual residence (Marcos)
Qualifications are continuing; an incumbent exercising his office elsewhere cannot claim a new domicile (Mangudadatu)
His new domicile begins only when he leaves that office (Mangudadatu)
src: Aquino v. COMELEC; Marcos v. COMELEC; Mangudadatu v. COMELEC (2025)

title: Second-placer rule after Mangudadatu
ask: What is the rule when a winning candidate is disqualified, and why (Mangudadatu)?
items: The second placer is not proclaimed; the second-placer rule is abandoned
The office is treated as vacant and filled by succession (for local offices, the Local Government Code)
Reason: the runner-up lost and was not the electorate’s choice
Imposing an unchosen runner-up violates the right of suffrage
Maquiling and Chua’s proclamation of the next-ranked candidate is no longer good law on this point
src: Mangudadatu v. COMELEC (2025); Aquino v. COMELEC (Labo doctrine)

title: Regular elections and Bañas-Nograles
ask: What are the rules on the date of regular congressional elections (Art. VI, Sec. 8; Bañas-Nograles)?
items: Regular election: second Monday of May, unless otherwise provided by law
‘Unless otherwise provided by law’ covers a law fixing another date
It also covers a law delegating the setting of the date to COMELEC
COMELEC cannot on its own suspend a congressional election and reset it
A district created after the election period began applies at the next regular election
Resetting would give the winner less than the three-year term of Sec. 7
COMELEC’s administrative power over elections is bound by the Constitution
src: Art. VI, Sec. 8; Bañas-Nograles v. COMELEC (2019)

title: Special elections to fill vacancies
ask: What are the rules on special elections for vacancies in Congress (Art. VI, Sec. 9; RA 6645 as amended by RA 7166)?
items: A special election ‘may be called’ to fill the vacancy, in the manner prescribed by law
The one elected serves only the unexpired term
Applies to a permanent vacancy at least one year before the expiration of the term
COMELEC calls and holds it not earlier than 60 nor later than 90 days after the vacancy
Senate vacancy: held simultaneously with the next succeeding regular election
A law fixing the special election with the regular election is itself the call; lack of separate notice not fatal (Tolentino)
House vacancy: COMELEC must call it and give notice, or it is void (Gatmaytan, reading Tolentino)
Voters have standing to question the validity of an election (Tolentino)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 9; RA 6645; RA 7166, Sec. 4; Tolentino v. COMELEC (2004); Hagedorn (2025)

title: Hagedorn v. House: special election points
ask: What did Hagedorn v. House of Representatives (2025) hold, including how RA 7166 changed RA 6645?
items: Mandamus does not lie against the House: Sec. 9 says ‘may’, and a resolution is discretionary under its rules
Mandamus lies against COMELEC: it must call and hold the special election within 60–90 days
RA 7166 deleted RA 6645’s requirement of a House or Senate resolution certifying the vacancy
Keeping the certification would defeat the mandatory 60-to-90-day period
Reckoning changed: from one year (House) or 18 months (Senate) before the next regular election to one year before the term expires
The power and duty to call now rest with COMELEC, without any positive act of Congress
COMELEC may rely on official press releases, or a certification from the Speaker or Secretary-General
src: Hagedorn v. House of Representatives (2025); RA 6645; RA 7166, Sec. 4

title: Parts of Art. VI, Sec. 16
ask: What are the five subjects covered by Art. VI, Sec. 16 (organization of each House)?
items: (1) Election of officers: Senate President and Speaker; other officers
(2) Quorum, adjournment from day to day, and compelling attendance
(3) Rules of proceedings and discipline of Members
(4) Journal and Record
(5) Adjournment: limits without the other House’s consent
src: Art. VI, Sec. 16(1)–(5)

title: Numbers to memorize in Sec. 16
ask: What vote, number or period does each part of Art. VI, Sec. 16 require?
items: Senate President and Speaker: majority vote of all its respective Members
Quorum: a majority of each House
A smaller number may adjourn from day to day and compel attendance of absent Members
Suspend or expel: concurrence of two-thirds of all its Members
Suspension: shall not exceed sixty days
Yeas and nays entered in the Journal: at the request of one-fifth of the Members present
Neither House may adjourn for more than three days without the other’s consent
src: Art. VI, Sec. 16(1)–(5)
hook: Only the Journal clause uses ‘Members present’; the others count ‘all’ the Members.

title: Election of officers of each House
ask: What are the rules on electing the officers of each House (Sec. 16(1); Santiago v. Guingona; Baguilat)?
items: Only the Senate President and Speaker are constitutionally elected: majority vote of all respective Members
Each House chooses such other officers as it deems necessary
How other officers (e.g., minority leader) are chosen is for each House’s rules, not the Court
Those who did not vote for the winner do not ipso facto form the ‘minority’ (Santiago)
No law or rule makes the losing candidate the minority leader (Santiago)
A ‘long-standing tradition’ creates no enforceable duty; mandamus does not lie (Baguilat)
The Court has jurisdiction to check a constitutional violation but defers absent grave abuse (Santiago)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 16(1); Santiago v. Guingona (1998); Baguilat v. Alvarez (2017)

title: Quorum rules
ask: What are the rules on quorum (Sec. 16(2); Avelino; Tinio)?
items: Quorum: a majority of each House
Base: members within the chamber’s coercive jurisdiction (Avelino)
Avelino: one senator abroad left a base of 23; 12 was a majority and a quorum
Absent members still in the country count in the base
A smaller number may adjourn from day to day and compel attendance, as the House provides
Once established, quorum is presumed to continue unless challenged under the House’s rules (Tinio)
The Journal and enrolled bill control over unauthenticated videos and photos (Tinio)
Quorum is not the vote to elect: Senate President and Speaker need a majority of all Members
A detained member is still counted as a Member but cannot be compelled to attend (Jalosjos)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 16(2); Avelino v. Cuenco (1949); Tinio v. Duterte (2023); People v. Jalosjos

title: Exceptions to non-interference in internal rules
ask: Courts generally do not enforce Congress’s internal rules (Arroyo v. De Venecia). What are the exceptions?
items: A constitutional requirement is involved: quorum, voting, or publication where required (Pimentel)
Rights of third parties are affected (Pacete)
Arbitrary and improvident use of rule-making amounting to denial of due process (Pimentel)
Grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction (expanded judicial review)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 16(3); Arroyo v. De Venecia; Pimentel v. Senate Committee of the Whole; Pacete v. CA
hook: General rule (Osmeña, quoted in Arroyo): parliamentary rules are procedural and may be waived.

title: Pimentel and Pacete points
ask: What did Pimentel v. Senate Committee of the Whole and Pacete v. Commission on Appointments hold?
items: Senate rule-making is subject to the Constitution’s quorum, voting and publication imperatives (Pimentel)
The Constitution does not require internal rules to be published unless the rules themselves say so (Pimentel)
The Committee of the Whole’s own rules required publication, so it had to publish before proceeding (Pimentel)
Referral to the Committee of the Whole was an internal Senate matter (Pimentel)
An unacted motion to reconsider a confirmation does not set it aside (Pacete)
Only a majority of CA members present can reopen and recall a confirmation; one member cannot (Pacete)
src: Pimentel v. Senate Committee of the Whole (2011); Pacete v. Commission on Appointments (1971)

title: Valid suspension or expulsion of a Member
ask: What are the requisites of a valid suspension or expulsion of a Member (Sec. 16(3))?
items: Ground: disorderly behavior, as the House itself determines (Osmeña)
Vote: concurrence of two-thirds of all its Members, not just those present
Suspension: not more than sixty days
Expulsion: no cap, the gravest penalty
Due process: notice and an opportunity to be heard
No criminal conviction required; discipline is distinct from criminal liability
src: Art. VI, Sec. 16(3); Osmeña v. Pendatun; Pimentel v. Senate Committee of the Whole

title: Penalties a House may impose on Members
ask: What penalties may a House impose on a Member for disorderly behavior?
items: Deletion of unparliamentary remarks from the record
Censure or reprimand
Fine
Imprisonment (listed in the class reviewer)
Suspension: two-thirds of all Members; at most sixty days
Expulsion: two-thirds of all Members
src: Art. VI, Sec. 16(3); House and Senate rules; DG reviewer
hook: Only suspension and expulsion need two-thirds of all Members; lesser penalties fall under the general power to ‘punish’.

title: Osmeña v. Pendatun points
ask: What are the key points of Osmeña v. Pendatun (1960)?
items: The speech privilege protects from being questioned ‘in any other place’, not in the Member’s own House
Purpose: fullest liberty of speech, protected from the resentment of the powerful
The privilege is not absolute
What is ‘disorderly behavior’ is for the House to decide; the Court will not review it
Taking up other business first does not waive the power to discipline; rules may be waived
The power to suspend is an inherent legislative prerogative, though the 1935 text named only expulsion
The 15-month suspension stood; the 1987 text now caps suspension at sixty days
Alejandrino distinguished: it involved an appointive senator under the Jones Law
src: Osmeña v. Pendatun (1960)

title: Alejandrino v. Quezon points
ask: What are the key points of Alejandrino v. Quezon (1924), and why may it be bad law?
items: Mandamus will not lie to compel the legislature to reinstate a suspended member; no power of coercion
The Senate could punish an appointive senator for disorderly behavior but not expel him
A one-year suspension of an appointive senator was a qualified expulsion: his district silenced, seat unfillable
Johnson, dissenting: courts may rule on positive acts of another branch that deprive persons of rights
Possibly bad law: no appointive legislators remain
Possibly bad law: the 1987 text expressly allows suspension (two-thirds, sixty days)
Possibly bad law: expanded judicial review now reaches grave abuse by Congress
src: Alejandrino v. Quezon (1924); DG reviewer

title: Preventive suspension by courts vs discipline by the House
ask: What are the differences between a court’s preventive suspension under RA 3019 and a chamber’s suspension under Sec. 16(3)?
items: Imposed by: the Sandiganbayan or court vs. the Member’s own House
Basis: RA 3019, Sec. 13 vs. Art. VI, Sec. 16(3)
Nature: precautionary, not a penalty vs. punitive
Trigger: mandatory once a valid information is filed vs. disorderly behavior
Vote: none vs. two-thirds of all Members
Length: up to 90 days (jurisprudence) vs. not more than sixty days
Purpose: keep the accused from intimidating witnesses, tampering with records or further malfeasance vs. discipline
src: De Venecia v. Sandiganbayan (2002); Santiago v. Sandiganbayan (2001); Art. VI, Sec. 16(3)

title: Arguments in a Teves-type expulsion
ask: In an expulsion like Teves’s (2023 Q1), what are the arguments for the House and for the Member?
items: For the House: no conviction is needed to expel
For the House: the Court defers on what counts as disorderly behavior (Osmeña)
For the Member: two prior sixty-day suspensions for the same absence; expulsion evades the cap and punishes twice
For the Member: an Executive terrorist designation or a personal video is not disorderly behavior as a Member
For the Member: due process (notice and hearing) must be observed
src: Art. VI, Sec. 16(3); Osmeña v. Pendatun; 2023 midterm Q1

title: Journal and Record duties
ask: What does Art. VI, Sec. 16(4) require of each House regarding its Journal and Record?
items: Keep a Journal of its proceedings
Publish it from time to time
Except parts that, in its judgment, affect national security
Enter the yeas and nays on any question at the request of one-fifth of the Members present
Keep a Record of its proceedings (a verbatim account of plenary proceedings)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 16(4)

title: Matters that must be entered in the Journal
ask: What matters does the Constitution require to be entered in the Journal?
items: Yeas and nays on the third and final reading of a bill (Art. VI, Sec. 26(2))
The President’s veto message, entered at large (Art. VI, Sec. 27(1))
Yeas and nays on repassing a vetoed bill (Art. VI, Sec. 27(1))
Yeas and nays on any question at the request of one-fifth of the Members present (Art. VI, Sec. 16(4))
The vote of each Member of the House on impeachment (Art. XI, Sec. 3(3))
src: Art. VI, Secs. 16(4), 26(2), 27(1); Art. XI, Sec. 3(3); Morales v. Subido
hook: Only matters affecting national security may be withheld from publication.

title: Enrolled bill vs Journal: the rules
ask: What are the rules on the enrolled bill doctrine and the probative value of the Journal?
items: Enrolled bill: signatures of the Senate President and Speaker plus the secretaries’ certification are conclusive of due enactment (CoTeSCUP)
The doctrine is court-made, grounded on respect for a coequal branch
Journal is conclusive on what it records; no extrinsic evidence (Pons)
Pons: courts take judicial notice of Journals; laws must rest on permanent records, not witnesses’ memory
On conflict, the enrolled bill prevails over the Journal (Casco; Morales)
Except matters the Constitution requires in the Journal: there the Journal may be consulted (Morales)
Exception: if presiding officers withdraw their signatures, there is no enrolled bill; consult the Journal (Astorga)
Astorga: approval by Congress, not signatures, makes a law; certification cannot cure a defect
Errors in an enrolled bill are corrected by amendment, not judicial decree (Morales)
src: CoTeSCUP (2018); U.S. v. Pons; Morales v. Subido; Astorga v. Villegas; Tinio v. Duterte

title: Limits on adjournment (Sec. 16(5))
ask: What are the elements of the adjournment rule in Art. VI, Sec. 16(5)?
items: Applies during the sessions of Congress
Neither House, without the consent of the other,
may adjourn for more than three days,
nor to any other place than that in which the two Houses are sitting
src: Art. VI, Sec. 16(5)

title: Regular and special sessions (Sec. 15)
ask: What are the elements of Art. VI, Sec. 15 on regular and special sessions?
items: Congress convenes once every year
On the fourth Monday of July, unless a different date is fixed by law
Continues in session for such number of days as it may determine
Until thirty days before the opening of its next regular session
Exclusive of Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays
The President may call a special session at any time
src: Art. VI, Sec. 15

title: Occasions for joint sessions
ask: On what four occasions does Congress meet in joint session, and how does it vote?
items: Declaring the existence of a state of war: two-thirds of both Houses, voting separately (Art. VI, Sec. 23(1))
Canvassing the votes for President and Vice-President, in joint public session (Art. VII, Sec. 4)
Revoking or extending martial law or the suspension of the writ: majority of all Members, voting jointly (Art. VII, Sec. 18)
The President’s address at the opening of the regular session (Art. VII, Sec. 23)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 23(1); Art. VII, Secs. 4, 18, 23; DG reviewer

title: Votes requiring a majority of all Members
ask: Which acts require a majority of ALL the Members (not just those present)?
items: Electing the Senate President and the Speaker (Art. VI, Sec. 16(1))
Commission on Appointments rulings: majority vote of all its Members (Art. VI, Sec. 18)
Passing a law granting a tax exemption: majority of all Members of Congress (Art. VI, Sec. 28(4))
Revoking or extending martial law or suspension of the writ: majority of all Members, voting jointly (Art. VII, Sec. 18)
src: Art. VI, Secs. 16(1), 18, 28(4); Art. VII, Sec. 18
hook: Contrast quorum (‘a majority of each House’, Avelino) and the one-fifth of Members ‘present’ for yeas and nays.

title: Votes requiring two-thirds
ask: Which acts of Congress or a House require a two-thirds vote, and two-thirds of what?
items: Suspending or expelling a Member: two-thirds of all its Members (Art. VI, Sec. 16(3))
Declaring a state of war: two-thirds of both Houses in joint session, voting separately (Art. VI, Sec. 23(1))
Overriding a veto: two-thirds of all the Members of each House (Art. VI, Sec. 27(1))
Concurring in a treaty: at least two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate (Art. VII, Sec. 21)
Calling a constitutional convention: two-thirds of all the Members of Congress (Art. XVII, Sec. 3)
src: Art. VI, Secs. 16(3), 23(1), 27(1); Art. VII, Sec. 21

title: Salaries of Members (Sec. 10)
ask: What are the elements of the salary rule in Art. VI, Sec. 10 and the rulings applying it?
items: Salaries of Senators and Representatives are determined by law
An increase may be enacted, but cannot take effect immediately
It takes effect only after the expiration of the full term of all Members of the Senate and House approving it
‘All the Members’ means both chambers together (PHILCONSA: RA 4134 not before Dec. 30, 1969)
Purpose: delay deters legislators from voting themselves raises (PHILCONSA)
Retirement gratuity is compensation; computing it on an unreceivable raise is an indirect increase (Ligot)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 10; PHILCONSA v. Mathay (1966); Ligot v. Mathay (1974)

title: Privilege from arrest: elements and limits
ask: What are the elements and limits of the privilege from arrest (Art. VI, Sec. 11)?
items: Holder: a Senator or Member of the House
Offense punishable by not more than six years imprisonment
While Congress is in session (regular or special); actual attendance not required
Not covered: offenses punishable by more than six years
Never exempts a convicted or lawfully detained Member (Jalosjos; Trillanes)
The chamber’s Sec. 16 powers do not include shielding a Member from law enforcement (‘protective custody’)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 11; People v. Jalosjos; Trillanes v. Pimentel; 2026 news (dela Rosa)

title: History of the privilege from arrest
ask: How did the privilege from arrest differ under the 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions (Jalosjos)?
items: 1935: all offenses except treason, felony and breach of the peace; during attendance at sessions and going to and from
1973: offenses punishable by not more than six years; during attendance at sessions
1973: the Batasan had to surrender the member within 24 hours after adjournment
1987: offenses punishable by not more than six years; while Congress is in session, attendance not required
src: People v. Jalosjos (2000)

title: Why election does not free a detained legislator
ask: What reasons did Jalosjos and Trillanes give for refusing to let a detained legislator attend sessions?
items: Voters elected him knowing of his confinement and its legal restraints
The popular mandate cannot override lawful penal and procedural restraints
Temporary leave is for emergencies; attending sessions five days a week would make him a free man
High office is not a substantial distinction lifting him out of the class of prisoners (equal protection)
Detainees, like convicts, cannot hold office or practise a profession while detained (People v. Maceda)
Applies to pre-trial detainees charged with reclusion perpetua offenses where evidence of guilt is strong (Trillanes)
src: People v. Jalosjos (2000); Trillanes IV v. Pimentel (2008)

title: Acts protected by the speech and debate clause
ask: What four kinds of acts are protected by the speech and debate privilege (Jimenez v. Cabangbang)?
items: Speeches delivered on the floor of Congress while in session
Statements made or votes cast in the halls of Congress while in session
Bills introduced in Congress, whether in session or not
Other official acts, inside or outside Congress, in the official discharge of duties as members of Congress or its committees
src: Art. VI, Sec. 11; Jimenez v. Cabangbang (1966)

title: Limits of the speech and debate privilege
ask: What are the limits of the speech and debate privilege?
items: Covers only legislative acts: it attaches because the statement furthers legislation, not because a lawmaker said it
Not covered: an open letter published in newspapers during recess (Jimenez)
Not covered: press releases and media interviews, which are ‘political in nature, rather than legislative’ (Trillanes v. Castillo-Marigomen)
Protects only from being questioned ‘in any other place’, not in the Member’s own House (Osmeña)
Discipline for floor speech belongs to the chamber, not the courts (Pobre)
Protects speech in Congress or its committees, not other conduct (Pobre, DG note)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 11; Jimenez; Trillanes v. Castillo-Marigomen (2018); Osmeña; Pobre v. Defensor-Santiago (2009)

title: Disqualifications of Members (Secs. 13–14)
ask: What are the five disqualifications or prohibitions on Members of Congress under Art. VI, Secs. 13 and 14?
items: Incompatible office: no other government office or employment (incl. GOCCs and subsidiaries) during term without forfeiting seat
Forbidden office: no appointment to an office created, or whose emoluments were increased, during the term for which elected
No personal appearance as counsel before courts, Electoral Tribunals, quasi-judicial and other administrative bodies
No direct or indirect financial interest in any government contract, franchise or special privilege during the term
No intervention in any matter before a government office for pecuniary benefit or where he may be called to act on account of office
src: Art. VI, Secs. 13–14; DG reviewer

title: Incompatible office vs forbidden office
ask: What are the differences between an incompatible office and a forbidden office under Art. VI, Sec. 13?
items: Source: first sentence of Sec. 13 vs. second sentence
Scope: any other government office or employment, incl. GOCCs and subsidiaries vs. only offices created or with increased emoluments during his term
Effect: he may accept but forfeits his seat vs. he cannot be appointed at all
Resignation: giving up the seat allows him to hold it vs. resigning does not cure the bar for the term for which elected
Forfeiture is automatic on assuming the other office (Adaza: taking the legislative oath vacated the governorship)
Contrast Art. IX-B, Sec. 7: an elective official is ineligible for any appointment during tenure; resigning after appointment does not cure (Flores v. Drilon)
The 1987 text has no Cabinet exception, unlike the 1973 rule applied in Adaza
src: Art. VI, Sec. 13; Adaza v. Pacana (1985); Art. IX-B, Sec. 7; Liban v. Gordon

title: Liban v. Gordon and RA 10530
ask: What did Liban v. Gordon hold, and how did RA 10530 settle its issues?
items: The PNRC chairmanship is not a government office, so Senator Gordon kept his seat
Reason: the Chairman is elected by a private-sector-controlled Board, not appointed by the President or a department head
The PNRC is sui generis, an auxiliary of government, not a GOCC
2009 voiding of parts of RA 95 (special charter for a private corporation) was reversed in 2011
Reversal grounds: RA 95’s validity was not the lis mota, and the PNRC is not an ordinary private corporation
RA 10530: the PNRC is an independent, autonomous, non-governmental organization auxiliary to government in the humanitarian field
So its chairmanship is not a Sec. 13 government office, and its charter is not barred by Art. XII, Sec. 16
src: Liban v. Gordon (2009, 2011); RA 10530 (2013); 2024 midterm Q4

title: Ban on appearing as counsel (Sec. 14)
ask: Before which bodies may a Member not personally appear as counsel, and what do Puyat and Pangilinan add?
items: Any court of justice
The Electoral Tribunals
Quasi-judicial bodies
Other administrative bodies
Cannot be evaded by buying token shares to intervene as a ‘stockholder’ (Puyat: ten shares bought after objection)
A stockholder intervening for his own genuine interest ordinarily is not appearing as counsel (Puyat)
De Lima’s request to argue as a party was denied because of her detention, not Sec. 14 (Pangilinan v. Cayetano)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 14; Puyat v. De Guzman (1982); Pangilinan v. Cayetano (Notice, 2018)

title: Disclosure and accountability duties of Members
ask: What disclosure and accountability duties apply to Members of Congress?
items: Upon assumption of office, full disclosure of their financial and business interests (Art. VI, Sec. 12)
Notify their House of a potential conflict of interest from filing a bill they author (Art. VI, Sec. 12)
SALN under oath, disclosed to the public, upon assumption and as often as required by law (Art. XI, Sec. 17)
Congress’s books are preserved, open to the public and audited by COA (Art. VI, Sec. 20)
COA publishes annually an itemized list of amounts paid to and expenses incurred for each Member (Art. VI, Sec. 20)
src: Art. VI, Secs. 12, 20; Art. XI, Sec. 17; DG reviewer
